steps.body: A function is a machine: f(x) = 3x + 4 takes x, multiplies by 3, then adds 4. Its inverse is the machine that undoes it — and undoing has a direction. Shoes went on last, so they come off first: f⁻¹ must reverse the steps in the OPPOSITE order, and flip each one as it goes.
Build your first inverse from the parts in the tray.

predict.prompt: f multiplies by 3, then adds 4. Which machine undoes it?

options.label: Divide by 3, then subtract 4 — undo each step in order
Subtract 4, then divide by 3 — undo the LAST step first
Multiply by 3, then add 4 — run the same machine again

predict.reveal: Undo the last step first. The + 4 was the final thing f did, so it's the first thing f⁻¹ must remove: subtract 4, THEN divide by 3. Undoing in the original order leaves the 4 trapped inside the ×3.

widget.prompt: f(x) = 3x + 4. Build f⁻¹ by placing undo-steps into the track — last step first.
widget.successFeedback: That's f⁻¹: subtract 4, then divide by 3 — so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 4)/3. Watch the sample value travel out and come straight back.
widget.forwardOrderFeedback: Those are the right two undo-steps, but in the order f applied them. An inverse runs the chain BACKWARDS: the + 4 happened last, so removing it must happen first.
widget.unflippedFeedback: Right order, but a step was copied instead of undone. Each card must be the OPPOSITE of the step it reverses: × 3 is undone by ÷ 3, + 4 by − 4.
widget.missFeedback: Read f left to right: ×3, then +4. Now build the track right to left, flipping each step as you go.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents inverse undo.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for inverse undo must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines inverse undo.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: f adds 5 first and doubles last, so f⁻¹ halves first and subtracts 5 last: f⁻¹(x) = x/2 − 5.
Reverse the order AND flip each step: the ×2 (last on) comes off first as ÷2; the +5 (first on) comes off last as −5.

widget.prompt: f(x) = 2(x + 5) — add 5, then multiply by 2. Build f⁻¹.
widget.successFeedback: f⁻¹(x) = x/2 − 5. The doubling was f's last act, so undoing it is f⁻¹'s first.
widget.forwardOrderFeedback: Right undo-steps, wrong direction — that track undoes the +5 before the ×2, but the ×2 is wrapped AROUND the +5. Unwrap from the outside in.
widget.unflippedFeedback: The order is right, but at least one card repeats f's step instead of reversing it. Flip it: × becomes ÷, + becomes −.
widget.missFeedback: f's chain is: +5, then ×2. Build the reverse, flipping each: ÷2 first, −5 second.

steps.body: This is why the textbook rule works. 'Swap x and y, then solve for y' is just this machine run in symbols: solving for y peels operations off from the outside in — the reversed, flipped chain you've been building by hand.
Three steps now. The middle step is where forward-order mistakes hide.

widget.prompt: f(x) = (3x + 4)/2 — multiply by 3, add 4, divide by 2. Build f⁻¹.
widget.successFeedback: f⁻¹(x) = (2x − 4)/3. Three layers, unwrapped outside-in: the ÷2 came off first as ×2, and the ×3 — f's very first move — came off last.
widget.forwardOrderFeedback: Right three undo-steps, but running forwards. f wrapped x in three layers; the OUTERMOST layer (÷2) has to come off first, and the innermost (×3) last.
widget.unflippedFeedback: The direction is right — now flip every card. Any step copied straight from f puts the layer back ON instead of taking it off.
widget.missFeedback: List f's steps in order: ×3, +4, ÷2. Reverse the list and flip each entry: ×2, −4, ÷3.

steps.body: Reverse this one without the warm-up.
explanationVariants: f subtracts 5 then multiplies by 4, so f⁻¹ divides by 4 then adds 5: f⁻¹(x) = x/4 + 5.
Outside layer off first: the ×4 wraps everything, so ÷4 leads; the −5 was innermost, so +5 closes.

widget.prompt: f(x) = 4(x − 5) — subtract 5, then multiply by 4. Build f⁻¹.
widget.successFeedback: f⁻¹(x) = x/4 + 5. Divide away the outer ×4 first, then restore the 5 that was taken.
widget.forwardOrderFeedback: Those cards undo f's steps in f's own order — the +5 can't come first while the ×4 is still wrapped around it. Peel the outside layer first.
widget.unflippedFeedback: Right order; now invert each card. A −5 in the track repeats f's subtraction — the undo is +5.
widget.missFeedback: f: −5, then ×4. Reverse and flip: ÷4 first, +5 second.

steps.body: From machine to notation: use the inverse you'd build, but answer with a number.
explanationVariants: Check it forwards: f(5) = 3·5 + 4 = 19, so f⁻¹ must send 19 back to 5.

commonErrors.feedback: That's f(19) = 3·19 + 4 — the machine run FORWARDS. f⁻¹(19) asks which input f sends to 19: undo it, (19 − 4)/3 = 5.
That divided by 3 before subtracting 4 — undoing f's steps in f's own order. The + 4 was applied last, so it's removed first: (19 − 4)/3 = 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Undo last-step-first: subtract 4 (19 − 4 = 15), then divide by 3: f⁻¹(19) = 5.

steps.body: Four layers deep. Every decoy in the tray is a real mistake waiting to be picked.
explanationVariants: f: ×2, +6, ÷4, −1. Reverse and flip every layer: +1, ×4, −6, ÷2 — so f⁻¹(x) = (4(x + 1) − 6)/2.
The last thing f did (−1) is the first thing f⁻¹ repairs (+1); the first thing f did (×2) is the last thing f⁻¹ removes (÷2).
hints: Which operation did f perform LAST? That's the only one f⁻¹ may touch first.
Write f's chain, reverse the list, then flip each entry: − becomes +, ÷ becomes ×.
The track reads: + 1, × 4, − 6, ÷ 2. Place them in exactly that order and run the sample value to confirm it returns.

widget.prompt: f(x) = (2x + 6)/4 − 1. Its chain: multiply by 2, add 6, divide by 4, subtract 1. Build f⁻¹.
widget.successFeedback: All four layers, unwrapped in perfect reverse: +1, ×4, −6, ÷2. The sample value goes out through f and comes straight home through your track.
widget.forwardOrderFeedback: Every card is a genuine undo-step — but the track runs in f's direction. Four layers deep, the rule is unchanged: outermost layer off first.
widget.unflippedFeedback: The direction is right, but at least one layer is being re-applied instead of removed. Check each card against the step it faces: it must be the opposite.
widget.missFeedback: f's chain: ×2, +6, ÷4, −1. Reverse it and flip every step: +1, ×4, −6, ÷2.

takeaways: An inverse reverses the ORDER of the steps and flips each one — last on, first off, like shoes and socks.
The two classic mistakes are now visible moves: undoing in f's own order, and reversing without flipping. The sample value catches both — it only comes home when both are right.

steps.body: Reverse the order, flip each step — the whole of inverse-building in one motion.
